group.title: Advanced finance
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: One of several portions into which an amount of money or a loan is divided.
examples: The loan will be paid in three {tranches} as each stage is finished.
wrong: The tranche was the whole loan, paid in one single sum.

words.meaning: The state of being able to pay all your debts.
examples: The auditors raised doubts about the insurer’s {solvency}.
wrong: Its solvency meant it could not pay any of its debts.

words.meaning: Unable to pay what you owe.
examples: The airline was declared {insolvent} and stopped flying.
wrong: The insolvent company paid all its debts with ease.

words.meaning: Buying something in one market and selling it at once in another for a higher price.
examples: Traders profited through {arbitrage} between the two exchanges.
wrong: Arbitrage means buying and selling at exactly the same price everywhere.

words.meaning: To reduce the risk of loss by making a balancing investment.
examples: Farmers {hedge} against falling prices by selling their crop in advance.
wrong: He hedged his bets by putting all his money on one horse.

words.meaning: A financial contract whose value depends on another asset, such as a share or currency.
examples: The bank lost billions on complex {derivatives} linked to housing loans.
wrong: A derivative is a simple coin that has value on its own.

words.meaning: Contracts to buy or sell something at a fixed price on a future date.
examples: Oil {futures} rose sharply after the supply cut.
wrong: Futures are deals that are settled and paid for in the past.

words.meaning: Trading borrowed shares: you sell them now, hoping to buy them back later for less.
examples: {Short selling} lets traders profit when a stock falls.
wrong: Short selling pays off only when the share price rises.

words.meaning: A long period when share prices are falling.
examples: Many investors lost heavily during the {bear market}.
wrong: In the bear market, prices climbed steadily for years.

words.meaning: A long period when share prices are rising.
examples: Pension funds grew fast during the long {bull market}.
wrong: In the bull market, share prices fell month after month.

words.meaning: How quickly and sharply prices go up and down.
examples: {Volatility} rose as markets reacted to the election.
wrong: The market’s volatility kept prices perfectly steady all year.

words.meaning: The income an investment earns, shown as a percentage of its price.
examples: The bond offers a {yield} of four percent a year.
wrong: The yield is the price you pay a broker to open an account.

words.meaning: One hundredth of one percent, used for interest rates and yields.
examples: The central bank raised rates by 25 {basis points}.
wrong: A basis point is a full ten percent rise in rates.

words.meaning: Spreading money across different investments to reduce risk.
examples: {Diversification} protected her savings when one sector crashed.
wrong: His diversification meant putting everything into one stock.

words.meaning: Profit made by selling an asset for more than you paid.
examples: She paid tax on the {capital gains} from selling her shares.
wrong: He reported capital gains after selling his house at a loss.

words.meaning: To pay off a debt, or spread a cost, in regular parts over time.
examples: The loan is {amortized} over twenty years.
wrong: They amortized the debt by paying it all on day one.

words.meaning: To build up gradually over time, especially interest or costs.
examples: Interest {accrues} daily on the unpaid balance.
wrong: The interest accrued, so the amount owed got smaller each day.

words.meaning: Property promised to a lender, which they can take if a loan is not repaid.
examples: He offered his house as {collateral} for the business loan.
wrong: The collateral is the money the lender gives you as a gift.

words.meaning: Bundling loans together and selling them to investors as securities.
examples: The {securitization} of mortgages spread risk across the world.
wrong: Securitization means keeping each loan locked in one bank’s safe.

words.meaning: To guarantee to buy unsold shares or to cover a risk for a fee.
examples: Three banks agreed to {underwrite} the share issue.
wrong: The bank underwrote the deal by refusing to accept any risk.

words.meaning: The first time a company offers its shares for sale to ordinary investors.
examples: The tech firm raised billions in its {initial public offering}.
wrong: The initial public offering was the company’s tenth share sale.

words.meaning: An estimate of what a company or asset is worth.
examples: The startup’s {valuation} doubled after the new contract.
wrong: The valuation told us the color of the company’s logo.

words.meaning: Describing large, reliable companies with a long record of success.
examples: Retirees prefer {blue-chip} stocks that pay steady dividends.
wrong: The blue-chip firm was a tiny, risky startup with no record.

words.meaning: Slow economic growth combined with high inflation and unemployment.
examples: The country suffered a decade of {stagflation}.
wrong: Stagflation is a boom with fast growth and stable prices.

words.meaning: When a central bank creates money to buy bonds and boost the economy.
examples: {Quantitative easing} pushed bond prices up and rates down.
wrong: Quantitative easing removes money from the economy to slow it.

words.meaning: Money owed by a national government.
examples: Rising {sovereign debt} worried investors in the eurozone.
wrong: Sovereign debt is a loan that a family owes to a shop.

words.meaning: The state of a failing company run by an official who sells assets to pay debts.
examples: The chain went into {receivership} after years of losses.
wrong: In receivership, the company was free to spend as it liked.

words.meaning: To close a business and sell its assets to pay its debts; to convert into cash.
examples: The court ordered the firm to {liquidate} its assets.
wrong: They liquidated the company by opening ten new branches.

words.meaning: The rapid movement of money out of a country by worried investors.
examples: Political unrest triggered {capital flight} and a falling currency.
wrong: Capital flight brought a wave of foreign money into the country.

words.meaning: An arrangement where a third party holds money until a deal is completed.
examples: The deposit is held in {escrow} until the house sale closes.
wrong: Money in escrow goes straight to the seller before any deal.

words.meaning: A broker’s demand for more money when a borrowed investment loses value.
examples: When prices fell, he faced a {margin call} he could not meet.
wrong: A margin call is a bonus paid when your investments rise.

words.meaning: The spread of financial trouble from one market or country to others.
examples: Regulators feared {contagion} from the collapse of one large bank.
wrong: Contagion kept the crisis neatly contained in one small firm.

words.meaning: The other side in a financial contract or trade.
examples: If the {counterparty} defaults, the bank may not get paid.
wrong: The counterparty is the same person who started the trade.

words.meaning: Preferring safer choices even if they earn less.
examples: {Risk-averse} savers kept their money in government bonds.
wrong: Being risk-averse, she gambled her savings on a new coin.

words.meaning: The extra return investors demand for accepting a greater chance of loss.
examples: Investors want a higher {risk premium} to lend to unstable countries.
wrong: The risk premium is lower for the riskiest loans.

words.meaning: A private investment pool using bold, complex strategies for wealthy clients.
examples: The {hedge fund} made a fortune betting against the housing market.
wrong: A hedge fund is a government savings scheme for small children.

words.meaning: Money invested in new, risky companies in exchange for a share.
examples: The startup raised {venture capital} to build its first factory.
wrong: Venture capital is a loan only for old, safe companies.

words.meaning: A graph comparing interest rates on bonds of different lengths.
examples: An inverted {yield curve} has often come before a recession.
wrong: The yield curve shows how many staff a bank employs each year.

words.meaning: To sell off a business, investment or asset.
examples: The university chose to {divest} from fossil fuel companies.
wrong: The firm divested by buying more shares in the same business.

words.meaning: A brief recovery in a falling price before it falls again.
examples: The rally turned out to be a {dead cat bounce}; prices sank the next week.
wrong: The dead cat bounce began a long, steady rise in prices.
